subject: Teaching Methodology
summary: Covers knowledge and curriculum concepts (types of knowledge, curriculum vs syllabus, hidden curriculum, Tyler's model, philosophical foundations), NCF 2005 and NCF 2022–23, the RTE Act 2009 with its key sections and Schedule norms, national policies (1968, 1986/1992, NEP 2020), schemes such as SSA and Samagra Shiksha, and the chronology of education commissions. Policy years, Act sections and commission names are high-frequency factual questions.

sections.heading: Knowledge and its kinds
sections.body:
**Knowledge** is justified understanding gained through experience, reasoning, testimony and reflection. **Information** is organised data; knowledge results when a learner interprets and connects information to what he/she already knows.
Common distinctions in education:
- **Propositional knowledge** ("knowing that") vs **procedural knowledge** ("knowing how") – the distinction drawn by philosopher Gilbert Ryle. Knowing the syntax of a loop is "knowing that"; writing a working loop is "knowing how".
- **A priori** (by reason, independent of experience – e.g. logic, mathematics) vs **a posteriori/empirical** (from experience and observation).
- **Tacit knowledge** (Michael Polanyi) – know-how that is hard to put into words, such as a programmer's sense of where a bug lies.
- **Local/indigenous knowledge** – knowledge of communities, crafts and environment; NCF 2005 asks schools to value it.
- **School knowledge vs everyday knowledge** – NCF 2005's first guiding principle is connecting knowledge to life outside the school.
**Constructivist view**: knowledge is not transmitted ready-made; learners construct it actively through experience and social interaction. This underlies NCF 2005 and NEP 2020.

sections.heading: Curriculum, syllabus and types of curriculum
sections.body:
- **Curriculum** – the totality of experiences a learner has under the guidance of the school: aims, content, methods, activities and evaluation, inside and outside the classroom (broad).
- **Syllabus** – a list/outline of topics to be taught in a subject in a given period (narrow, part of the curriculum).
- **Textbook** – one resource that presents the syllabus.
Types of curriculum:
- **Subject-centred** – organised around disciplines; **learner-centred** – around interests and needs of children; **activity/experience-centred** – learning by doing (Dewey); **core curriculum** – common essential learning for all.
- **Spiral curriculum** (Bruner) – topics revisited with increasing depth.
- **Hidden curriculum** – the unwritten values, norms and attitudes learned through school life (e.g. obedience, gender roles, punctuality); term coined by **Philip Jackson** (1968).
- **Null curriculum** (Elliot Eisner) – what schools do not teach, which also sends a message.
**Curriculum development models**: **Ralph Tyler (1949)** – a linear, objectives-based model built on four questions: what purposes (objectives), what experiences, how to organise them, how to evaluate. **Hilda Taba** – an inductive, "grassroots" model in which teachers develop units first.

sections.heading: Philosophical foundations of curriculum
sections.body: A curriculum reflects a view of what education is for. **Idealism** stresses ideas, values and the teacher as a model; **naturalism** puts the child's nature first; **pragmatism** values experience, activity and problem solving; **Indian thinkers** linked education with work, freedom, character and self-realisation. Constructivist frameworks such as NCF 2005 draw heavily on Dewey, Gandhi and Tagore.

sections.heading: National Curriculum Framework 2005
sections.body:
NCERT has brought out national curriculum frameworks in **1975, 1988, 2000 and 2005**, followed by the NEP-aligned frameworks of 2022–23.
**NCF 2005** was developed under a National Steering Committee chaired by **Prof. Yash Pal**. It drew on the report **"Learning Without Burden" (1993)**. Its **five guiding principles**:
- Connecting knowledge to life outside the school.
- Ensuring that learning shifts away from rote methods.
- Enriching the curriculum to provide for overall development of children rather than remaining textbook-centric.
- Making examinations more flexible and integrated with classroom life.
- Nurturing an over-riding identity informed by caring concerns within the democratic polity of the country.
Other key positions: a **constructivist** view of learning – the child as an active constructor of knowledge and the teacher as facilitator; **multilingualism** as a resource and use of the home language; reduction of curriculum load and exam stress; art, health, work and peace education as integral parts of the curriculum; respect for local knowledge; inclusion of all children.

sections.heading: NCF 2022–23 (Foundational Stage and School Education)
sections.body:
Following NEP 2020, two new frameworks were issued under a National Steering Committee chaired by **Dr K. Kasturirangan**:
- **NCF for the Foundational Stage (NCF-FS), 2022** – for children aged 3 to 8 (three years of pre-school/Balvatika plus Grades 1–2); emphasises play-based, activity-based learning and uses the Indian idea of the **Panchakosha** (five layers of development) to frame holistic development.
- **NCF for School Education (NCF-SE), 2023** – covers the 5+3+3+4 structure up to Grade 12.
Key features of NCF-SE 2023:
- Learning standards and competencies defined stage-wise; reduced content to allow deeper understanding.
- Board examinations to be offered **at least twice a year** so students can attempt their best performance; board exams test competencies rather than months of coaching and memorisation.
- Language learning with at least two of the three languages being **native to India**.
- Greater flexibility and choice in secondary stage subjects, with no hard separation between arts, science and commerce; vocational education, art and physical education given equal status.
- Integration of Indian knowledge systems, values and the local context.

sections.heading: RTE Act 2009: background and core rights
sections.body:
- **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002** inserted **Article 21A** (free and compulsory education for all children aged **6 to 14** as a fundamental right, in a manner the State may by law determine), substituted **Article 45** (early childhood care and education for children below 6) and added **Article 51A(k)** (duty of parents/guardians to provide opportunities for education to their child between 6 and 14).
- The **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009** is that law; it came into force on **1 April 2010**.
- **Free** means no fee, charge or expense that may prevent a child from completing elementary education; **compulsory** places the obligation on the government to ensure admission, attendance and completion.
- A child not admitted or who dropped out is to be admitted to an **age-appropriate class** and given **special training** (Section 4).
- Applies to elementary education: **Classes 1 to 8**.

sections.heading: RTE Act 2009: key sections and norms
sections.body: Section numbers are frequently asked. The Act places duties on the appropriate government, local authority, schools, teachers and parents. The most important provisions for teachers are listed below; note that Section 16 was changed by the **RTE (Amendment) Act, 2019**.

rows: Private unaided (and specified category) schools reserve at least 25% of entry-class seats for children of weaker sections and disadvantaged groups
No capitation fee and no screening procedure for admission
No denial of admission for lack of age proof
No holding back or expulsion till completion of elementary education (amended in 2019 to allow exams and detention in Classes 5 and 8)
Prohibition of physical punishment and mental harassment
School Management Committee: at least three-fourths parents/guardians; 50% of members women
Minimum teacher qualifications laid down by the academic authority (NCTE); basis of TET
Duties of teachers: regularity, punctuality, complete curriculum, assess learning, meet parents
No non-educational duties except census, disaster relief and elections
Curriculum and evaluation by academic authority; child-friendly, activity-based learning; CCE; mother tongue as far as practicable
No board examination till completion of elementary education

sections.heading: RTE Schedule norms
sections.body:
The **Schedule** to the RTE Act lays down minimum norms for every school:
- **Pupil–teacher ratio**: Primary (Classes 1–5) – up to 60 children: 2 teachers; 61–90: 3; 91–120: 4; 121–200: 5; above 150 children: 5 teachers plus a head teacher; above 200: PTR (excluding head teacher) not to exceed 40. Upper primary (Classes 6–8) – at least one teacher per class so that there is a teacher each for science and mathematics, social studies, and languages, with at least one teacher for every 35 children.
- **Working days**: at least **200** days (primary) and **220** days (upper primary) in an academic year.
- **Instructional hours**: **800** hours (primary) and **1000** hours (upper primary) per year.
- **Teacher working hours**: minimum **45 hours per week** including preparation.
- **Building**: all-weather building with at least one classroom per teacher, an office-cum-store-cum-head teacher's room, barrier-free access, separate toilets for boys and girls, safe drinking water, kitchen for mid-day meal, playground and boundary wall.
- Teaching–learning equipment, a library, and play and sports equipment.

sections.heading: National policies: 1968, 1986/1992 and NEP 2020
sections.body:
**NPE 1968** – first national policy, based on the Kothari Commission: free and compulsory education up to 14, **three-language formula**, improved teacher status, and spending to rise towards **6% of national income**.
**NPE 1986** (modified by the **Programme of Action, 1992**, after review by the Acharya Ramamurti Committee) – "Education for All"; **Operation Blackboard** for minimum facilities in primary schools; **Navodaya Vidyalayas**; DIETs for teacher education; open universities; non-formal education; emphasis on removing disparities.
**NEP 2020** – approved by the Union Cabinet on **29 July 2020**; drafted by a committee chaired by **Dr K. Kasturirangan**; replaced NPE 1986.
- **5+3+3+4** structure replacing 10+2: Foundational (ages 3–8), Preparatory (8–11, Grades 3–5), Middle (11–14, Grades 6–8), Secondary (14–18, Grades 9–12).
- Universal access to school education from age 3 to 18; **foundational literacy and numeracy** for all by Grade 3 (implemented through the **NIPUN Bharat** mission, 2021).
- Medium of instruction: home language/mother tongue/regional language **at least until Grade 5, preferably till Grade 8 and beyond**; three-language formula with flexibility.
- Vocational education and **coding from Grade 6**; 10-day bagless period.
- Assessment reform: Holistic Progress Card, PARAKH, easier board exams with two attempts.
- Teacher education: **4-year integrated B.Ed** to become the minimum degree qualification by 2030.
- Higher education: GER target of **50% by 2035**; multiple entry and exit; Academic Bank of Credit; HECI as single regulator (proposed).
- Public investment in education to reach **6% of GDP**; MHRD renamed **Ministry of Education**.

sections.heading: Schemes: SSA, RMSA, Samagra Shiksha and others
sections.body:
- **Mid-Day Meal Scheme (1995)** – cooked meal for school children to improve enrolment, attendance and nutrition; renamed and expanded as **PM POSHAN** (2021).
- **District Primary Education Programme (DPEP), 1994** – district-level planning for universal primary education.
- **Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), 2001** – flagship programme for **Universalisation of Elementary Education** (ages 6–14) in a time-bound manner; community ownership, bridging gender and social gaps, zero-rejection policy for children with special needs. After 2010 it became the main vehicle for implementing RTE.
- **Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (KGBV), 2004** – residential upper primary schools for girls from disadvantaged groups in educationally backward blocks.
- **Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA), 2009** – universal access to and quality of secondary education.
- **Samagra Shiksha (2018)** – integrated scheme subsuming **SSA, RMSA and Teacher Education**, covering pre-school to Class 12 as a continuum.
- **NIPUN Bharat (2021)** – National Initiative for Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy, for foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3.

workedExamples.problem: A primary school (Classes 1–5) has 135 children. Under the RTE Schedule, how many teachers are required? What if the enrolment rises to 180?
workedExamples.solution:
- 135 lies in the 121–200 band → **5 teachers**. It is not above 150, so a separate head teacher is not required by the norm.
- 180 lies in 121–200 and is above 150 → **5 teachers + 1 head teacher**.

workedExamples.problem: A private unaided school admits 80 children in Class 1. How many seats must be filled under RTE Section 12(1)(c)?
workedExamples.solution: - At least 25% of the entry-class strength: 0.25 × 80 = **20 seats** for children from weaker sections and disadvantaged groups in the neighbourhood.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the RTE provision violated: (a) a school conducts an interview of parents before admitting a child to Class 1; (b) a teacher gives paid tuition at home to students of his own school; (c) a child is refused admission because he has no birth certificate.
workedExamples.solution:
- (a) Screening procedure for admission → violates **Section 13**.
- (b) Private tuition by a teacher → violates **Section 28**.
- (c) Denial for lack of age proof → violates **Section 14**.

workedExamples.problem: Under NEP 2020, which stage and age group would a child in Grade 4 and a student in Grade 7 belong to?
workedExamples.solution:
- Grade 4: Grades 3–5 = **Preparatory stage**, ages about 8–11.
- Grade 7: Grades 6–8 = **Middle stage**, ages about 11–14.

workedExamples.problem: Arrange chronologically: Kothari Commission, Hunter Commission, Mudaliar Commission, Radhakrishnan Commission, Sadler Commission.
workedExamples.solution:
- Hunter Commission (1882)
- Sadler Commission (1917–19)
- Radhakrishnan Commission (1948–49)
- Mudaliar Commission (1952–53)
- Kothari Commission (1964–66)

pitfalls: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment in 2002; the RTE Act came in 2009 and into force on 1 April 2010.
RTE covers ages 6–14 (Classes 1–8); RPwD Act gives free education to children with benchmark disabilities from 6 to 18.
The 25% reservation is under Section 12(1)(c) and applies to the entry class of private unaided schools.
SMC: three-fourths parents, half of members women – do not reverse the fractions.
Radhakrishnan Commission dealt with university education; Mudaliar with secondary; Kothari was the comprehensive Education Commission.
Hunter Commission (1882) was the first education commission of India; Radhakrishnan (1948–49) was the first after independence.
NCF 2005 was chaired by Yash Pal; NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 by Kasturirangan.
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan was launched in 2001; RMSA in 2009; Samagra Shiksha in 2018.
Syllabus is a part of the curriculum, not the other way round.
Hidden curriculum is unwritten learning (values, norms); null curriculum is what is left out.
NEP 2020's mother-tongue medium is 'at least until Grade 5, preferably till Grade 8 and beyond' – not compulsory till Grade 12.
quickRevision: Curriculum = all school experiences; syllabus = list of content.
Hidden curriculum: Philip Jackson (1968); null curriculum: Eisner; spiral: Bruner.
NCF 2005: Yash Pal; five guiding principles; constructivism.
RTE Act 2009 in force from 1 April 2010; ages 6–14.
RTE Sec 12(1)(c): 25% seats; Sec 13: no capitation/screening; Sec 17: no corporal punishment.
RTE PTR: 30:1 primary, 35:1 upper primary; 200/220 days; 800/1000 hours.
NEP 2020: 5+3+3+4; 6% of GDP; GER 50% by 2035; coding from Grade 6.
SSA 2001; KGBV 2004; RMSA 2009; Samagra Shiksha 2018; NIPUN Bharat 2021.
Wood's Despatch 1854 = Magna Carta of English education in India.
Learning Without Burden: Yash Pal Committee, 1993.
